source_text: Πλὴν καὶ ἄκων ἐνέπεσεν ὁ Κέλσος εἰς τὸ μαρτυρεῖν τῷ νεώτερον εἶναι τὸν κόσμον καὶ οὐδέπω μυρίων ἐτῶν εἰπὼν καὶ Ἕλληνας ταῦτα νομίζειν ἀρχαῖα, ὡς πρεσβύτερα διὰ τοὺς κατακλυσμοὺς καὶ τὰς ἐκπυρώσεις οὐ τεθεωρήκασιν οὐδ᾿ ἀπομνημονεύουσιν. ἔστωσαν δὲ τῷ Κέλσῳ τοῦ περὶ τῶν ἐκπυρώσεων καὶ ἐξυδατώσεων μύθου διδάσκαλοι οἱ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν σοφώτατοι Αἰγύπτιοι, ὧν τῆς σοφίας ἴχνη ἄλογα ζῷα προσκυνούμενα καὶ λόγοι παριστάντες εὔλογον εἶναι καὶ ἀνακεχωρηκυῖάν τινα καὶ μυστικὴν τὴν τοιαύτην τοῦ θεοῦ θεραπείαν. κἂν μὲν Αἰγύπτιοι περὶ τῶν ζῴων σεμνύνοντες ἑαυτῶν τὸν λόγον θεολογίας φέρωσι, σοφοί εἰσιν· ἐὰν δὲ ὁ τῷ Ἰουδαίων συγκαταθέμενος νόμῳ καὶ νομοθέτῃ πάντα ἀναφέρῃ ἐπὶ τὸν τῶν ὅλων δημιουργὸν μόνον θεὸν. ἥττων εἶναι παρὰ Κέλσῳ καὶ τοῖς ὁμοίοις αὐτῷ λογίζεται τοῦ μὴ εἰς λογικὰ μόνον καὶ θνητὰ ζῷα ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς ἄλογα κατάγοντος τὴν θεότητα ὑπὲρ τὴν μυθικὴν μετενσωμάτωσιν. τὴν περὶ τῆς πιπτούσης ἀπὸ τῶν ἁψίδων τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ψυχῆς καὶ ἕως τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων, οὐ μόνον ἡμέρων ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀγριωτάτων. καταβαινούσης. καὶ ἐὰν μὲν Αἰγύπτιοι μυθολογῶσι, πιστεύονται πεφιλοσοφηκέναι δι᾿ αἰνιγμῶν καὶ ἀποῤῥήτων, ἐὰν δὲ Μω(??)σῆς ὅλῳ ἔθνει συγγράφων ἱστορίας καὶ νόμους αὐτοῖς καταλίπῃ. μῦθοι κενοὶ νομίζονται μηδ᾿ ἀλληγορίαν ἐπιδεχόμενοι οἱ λόγοι αὐτοῦ·
pass_a_gloss: But also Celsus unwillingly fell into testifying that the world is younger and not yet ten thousand years old, saying that Greeks think these things are ancient, as they have not observed nor remembered older things because of the floods and conflagrations. Let the most wise Egyptians according to him be the teachers of the myth about conflagrations and inundations, whose wisdom is indicated by irrational animals being worshiped and words presenting a logical thing and having retreated to some mystical service of God. And if Egyptians, honoring animals, bring their word to theology, they are wise; but if the one who has been laid down with the law and lawgiver of the Jews refers everything to the one God, creator of all. He is considered to be inferior by Celsus and those like him, because he leads divinity not only to rational and mortal animals but also to irrational ones, beyond the mythical transmigration. The thing about the soul falling from the vaults of heaven, and as far as irrational animals, not only tame but also wild, descending. And if Egyptians mythologize, they are believed to have philosophized through riddles and apothegms; but if Moses, writing history and laws for the whole nation, leaves them behind, his words are dismissed as empty myths that admit no allegory.
pass_b_english: Even so, Celsus inadvertently ends up testifying that the world is younger, not yet ten thousand years old, claiming that Greeks regard these things as ancient because they have neither observed nor remembered anything older, thanks to the floods and conflagrations. Let the Egyptians whom he considers the wisest serve as teachers of the myth about conflagrations and inundations; their wisdom is displayed in the worship of irrational animals and in arguments that present such practices as reasonable and as having retreated into a certain mystical service of God. If Egyptians honor animals and call their reasoning theology, they are deemed wise; but if the one who has aligned himself with the law and lawgiver of the Jews refers everything to the one God, the creator of all, he is judged inferior by Celsus and his like, because he brings the divine down not only to rational and mortal creatures but also to irrational ones, going beyond even mythical transmigration. This concerns the soul falling from the vaults of heaven and descending as far as irrational animals, not only tame but also wild. And if Egyptians mythologize, people believe they have philosophized through riddles and cryptic sayings; but if Moses writes history and laws for an entire nation and leaves them behind, his words are dismissed as empty myths that admit no allegory.
notes: The text appears to be damaged or incomplete in some places, as indicated by the '(??)' in 'Μω(??)σῆς'.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Greek text. Pass A and Pass B both correctly handle the complex syntax regarding the Egyptians and the comparison between them and the Mosaic lawgiver. The uncertainty in the source 'Μω(??)σῆς' is noted in the translator's notes. All clauses, including the description of the soul's descent and the nature of Egyptian wisdom, are preserved.
